claim: Starvation-induced hyperactivity is a behavioral trait observed across different wild-type fly strains, though its magnitude might differ.
source: In this present study, we first confirmed that starvation-induced hyperactivity was a behavioral trait observed across different wild-type fly strains, though its magnitude might differ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which displays results from multiple wild-type strains.

claim: The timing of the onset of starvation-induced hyperactivity might differ across different wild-type strains.
source: In addition, the timing of the onset of starvation-induced hyperactivity might differ across different wild-type strains, too. In some strains the response started in Day 1 after starvation while some started in Day 2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which displays temporal differences in behavioral responses across strains.

claim: HFD-fed flies exhibited further enhanced hyperactivity upon starvation in both Day 1 and Day 2 compared to ND-fed flies.
source: Compared to ND-fed flies, flies fed with HFD exhibited further enhanced hyperactivity upon starvation in both days (Figure 1B, E–F and H–I, orange).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, E-F, and H-I, which compares locomotor activity between ND and HFD-fed flies.

claim: The baseline activity of fed flies was not affected by HFD feeding.
source: Meanwhile, the baseline activity of fed flies was not affected by HFD feeding (Figure 1A–B, D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B, D, and G, which shows comparable baseline activity between ND and HFD-fed flies.

claim: The effect of HFD to enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity was dose-dependent.
source: We also compared the effect of adding 5%, 10%, and 20% coconut oil in ND and found that the effect of HFD to enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity was dose-dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, which compares different concentrations of coconut oil.

claim: HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly increased walking speed before locating food sources.
source: We found that HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly increased walking speed and significantly decreased latency before locating and occupying the food sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C from video recording-based food seeking assay.

claim: HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly decreased latency before locating and occupying food sources.
source: We found that HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly increased walking speed and significantly decreased latency before locating and occupying the food sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C from video recording-based food seeking assay.

claim: Total visits to food and the duration to stay on food remained unchanged in HFD-fed flies.
source: whereas their total visits to food and the duration to stay on food remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E from video recording-based food seeking assay.

claim: Coconut oil and lard, which were rich in saturated fat, significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity.
source: Coconut oil and lard, which were rich in saturated fat (Segarra et al., 2002), significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and cited literature on fat composition.

claim: Soybean oil, which was mostly unsaturated fat, did not affect starvation-induced hyperactivity.
source: In contrast, soybean oil, which was mostly unsaturated fat (Henkel et al., 2018), did not affect starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and cited literature on fat composition.

claim: High-sugar diet (HSD) did not enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity.
source: High-sugar diet (HSD) did not enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity, either (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: ND-fed and HFD-fed flies exhibited comparable feeding activity in the FLIC assay and the BARCODE assay.
source: In contrast, ND-fed and HFD-fed flies exhibited comparable feeding activity in the FLIC assay (Ro et al., 2014) and the BARCODE assay (Park et al., 2018; Figure 1J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and K using two different feeding assays, with citations to the methods.

claim: Flies' body weight was not affected by HFD.
source: However, flies' body weight was not affected by HFD, and their lipid storage was actually significantly elevated by HFD (Figure 1L and M)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L measuring body weight.

claim: Lipid storage was significantly elevated by HFD.
source: However, flies' body weight was not affected by HFD, and their lipid storage was actually significantly elevated by HFD (Figure 1L and M)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M measuring triglyceride storage.

claim: The energy expenditure of flies was not affected by HFD.
source: The energy expenditure of flies was not affected by HFD. Evidently, when fed ad libitum, the CO2 production of HFD-fed and ND-fed flies was comparable (Figure 1N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N measuring CO2 production as a proxy for energy expenditure.

claim: Upon 24 hr starvation, the body weight and lipid storage of both ND-fed and HFD-fed flies decreased.
source: Consistently, upon 24 hr starvation, the body weight and lipid storage of both ND-fed and HFD-fed flies decreased (Figure 1O and P)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O and P measuring body weight and lipid storage after starvation.

claim: Upon 24 hr starvation, the food consumption of ND-fed and HFD-fed flies increased in comparable manners.
source: whereas the food consumption of these two groups of flies increased in the MAFE assay, in comparable manners (Figure 1Q, note that flies exhibited no food ingestion in the MAFE assay when fed ad libitum) (Qi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1Q using the MAFE assay, with citation to the method.

claim: Five days of HFD feeding specifically enhances starvation-induced hyperactivity without altering flies' food intake and energy expenditure.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that five days of HFD feeding specifically enhances starvation-induced hyperactivity without altering flies' food intake and energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple experimental results presented in Figure 1.

claim: Starvation-induced hyperactivity of adult flies was driven by a specific group of OA neurons in the fly brain.
source: We showed in a previous study that starvation-induced hyperactivity of adult flies was driven by a specific group of OA neurons in the fly brain (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The activity of OA+ neurons is regulated in opposite directions by two groups of functionally antagonizing hormones, the hunger-induced hormone AKH and the satiety hormones DILPs.
source: As a hunger sensor, the activity of these OA+ neurons is regulated in opposite directions, by two groups of functionally antagonizing hormones, the hunger-induced hormone AKH and the satiety hormones DILPs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous work, as indicated by the context.

claim: ND-fed and HFD-fed flies showed comparable AKH and DILP2 mRNA production as revealed by both RNAseq and quantitative RT-PCR.
source: As shown in Figure 2A–B, ND-fed and HFD-fed flies showed comparable AKH and DILP2 mRNA production as revealed by both RNAseq (Figure 2A) and quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B using two different methods.

claim: Circulating AKH and DILP2 in flies' hemolymph were elevated and reduced upon starvation, respectively.
source: Moreover, circulating AKH and DILP2 in flies' hemolymph were elevated and reduced upon starvation, respectively (Figure 2C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D using dot blot analysis.

claim: The levels of circulating AKH and DILP2 remained unaffected by HFD feeding under both fed and starved conditions.
source: Nevertheless, their levels remained unaffected by HFD feeding under both fed and starved conditions, as shown by the dot blot using antibodies against AKH and DILP2 proteins (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D using dot blot analysis.

claim: AKHR mRNA levels remained unchanged after HFD feeding, as revealed by RNAseq and quantitative RT-PCR.
source: While AKHR mRNA levels remained unchanged after HFD feeding, as revealed by RNAseq and quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2E–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F using two different methods.

claim: AKHR protein was significantly elevated in the head tissue of HFD-fed flies vs. that of ND-fed flies.
source: AKHR protein was significantly elevated in the head tissue of HFD-fed flies vs. that of ND-fed flies, as demonstrated by western blot (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H using western blot analysis.

claim: The production of dInR was not affected by HFD at both the transcriptional and translational levels.
source: The production of dInR was not affected by HFD at both the transcriptional and translational levels (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-H using multiple methods.

claim: AKHR+ neurons in HFD-fed flies exhibited more robust calcium transients when stimulated with synthetic AKH than those in ND-fed flies in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, by using a calcium imaging setup with ex vivo brain preparations, we found that these AKHR+ neurons in HFD-fed flies exhibited more robust calcium transients when stimulated with synthetic AKH than those in ND-fed flies in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-K using calcium imaging.

claim: Blocking lysosome-mediated protein degradation by lysosome inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) and NH4Cl increased AKHR protein levels dramatically.
source: To examine this possibility, we ectopically expressed HA-tagged AKHR protein in cultured Drosophila S2 cells, and found that blocking lysosome-mediated protein degradation by lysosome inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) and NH4Cl increased AKHR protein levels dramatically, while MG132 treatment to disturb proteasome function exerted little effect (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B using cultured cells and pharmacological inhibitors.

claim: MG132 treatment to disturb proteasome function exerted little effect on AKHR protein levels.
source: To examine this possibility, we ectopically expressed HA-tagged AKHR protein in cultured Drosophila S2 cells, and found that blocking lysosome-mediated protein degradation by lysosome inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) and NH4Cl increased AKHR protein levels dramatically, while MG132 treatment to disturb proteasome function exerted little effect (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B using cultured cells and pharmacological inhibitors.

claim: AKHR may be mainly degraded via the lysosome pathway.
source: Therefore, AKHR may be mainly degraded via the lysosome pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that lysosome inhibitors but not proteasome inhibitors affect AKHR levels.

claim: Upon rapamycin treatment, HA-tagged AKHR protein was enriched in autophagosomes.
source: Notably, upon rapamycin treatment, HA-tagged AKHR protein was also enriched in these autophagosomes (Figure 3C, red).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C using immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: Inducing autophagy by both starvation and rapamycin resulted in significantly decreased AKHR protein levels in cultured S2 cells.
source: Moreover, inducing autophagy by both starvation and rapamycin resulted in significantly decreased AKHR protein levels in cultured S2 cells (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-E using cultured cells.

claim: HFD suppressed autophagy in the AKHR+ neurons, as evident by the relative decrease of membrane-associated ATG8-II upon HFD feeding.
source: Indeed, HFD suppressed autophagy in the AKHR+ neurons, as evident by the relative decrease of membrane-associated ATG8-II upon HFD feeding (GFP-ATG8-II/I, Figure 3F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G using western blot analysis of ATG8 processing.

claim: Specifically suppressing autophagy in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of two critical autophagy initiators ATG5 and ATG7, significantly enhanced AKHR accumulation in ND-fed flies.
source: Additionally, specifically suppressing autophagy in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of two critical autophagy initiators ATG5 and ATG7, significantly enhanced AKHR accumulation in ND-fed flies (Figure 3H–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I using genetic manipulation.

claim: RNAi knock-down of ATG5 and ATG7 in AKHR+ neurons both led to significantly enhanced calcium transients upon AKH administration in ND-fed flies.
source: Indeed, RNAi knock-down of ATG5 and ATG7 in AKHR+ neurons both led to significantly enhanced calcium transients upon AKH administration in ND-fed flies (Figure 4A–B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B using calcium imaging.

claim: Blocking autophagy in AKHR+ neurons via RNAi knock-down of ATG5 significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies without altering their baseline activity.
source: Consistent with these results, blocking autophagy in AKHR+ neurons via RNAi knock-down of ATG5 significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies without altering their baseline activity (Figure 4C–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-F using behavioral assays.

claim: HFD feeding did not further enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity when autophagy was suppressed by ATG5/7 knockdown.
source: In both conditions, HFD feeding did not further enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4), likely due to the suppression of autophagy by ATG5/7 knockdown.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, with inference about the mechanism.

claim: The head tissues of HFD-fed flies exhibited higher levels of p70S6K phosphorylation.
source: Indeed, the head tissues of HFD-fed flies exhibited higher levels of p70S6K phosphorylation (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that HFD activated TOR signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B using western blot analysis.

claim: Upon HFD feeding, AMPK signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AMPK) was suppressed.
source: We found that upon HFD feeding, AMPK signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AMPK) was suppressed, whereas AKT signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AKT) remained unaffected (Figure 5C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D using western blot analysis.

claim: Upon HFD feeding, AKT signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AKT) remained unaffected.
source: We found that upon HFD feeding, AMPK signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AMPK) was suppressed, whereas AKT signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AKT) remained unaffected (Figure 5C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D using western blot analysis.

claim: Pharmacological activation of TOR signaling by MHY and suppression of AMPK by dorsomorphin both resulted in AKHR accumulation in cultured S2 cells.
source: Indeed, pharmacological activation of TOR signaling by MHY and suppression of AMPK by dorsomorphin (dorso) both resulted in AKHR accumulation in cultured S2 cells, whereas suppression of TOR signaling by rapamycin and activation of AMPK by AICAR exerted the opposite effect (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F using cultured cells and pharmacological agents.

claim: Suppression of TOR signaling by rapamycin and activation of AMPK by AICAR exerted the opposite effect on AKHR accumulation.
source: Indeed, pharmacological activation of TOR signaling by MHY and suppression of AMPK by dorsomorphin (dorso) both resulted in AKHR accumulation in cultured S2 cells, whereas suppression of TOR signaling by rapamycin and activation of AMPK by AICAR exerted the opposite effect (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F using cultured cells and pharmacological agents.

claim: Dorsomorphin and rapamycin feeding led to increased and decreased AKH sensitivity in AKHR+ neurons, respectively.
source: Consistent with these in vitro results, dorso and rapamycin feeding led to increased and decreased AKH sensitivity in AKHR+ neurons, respectively (Figure 5G–H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-H using calcium imaging.

claim: Suppressing TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons by ectopic expression of dominant negative TORTED resulted in significantly decreased starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
source: Indeed, suppressing TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons by ectopic expression of dominant negative TORTED (Hennig and Neufeld, 2002) resulted in significantly decreased starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies, and these flies did not respond to HFD (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claim: Flies expressing TORTED in AKHR+ neurons did not respond to HFD.
source: Indeed, suppressing TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons by ectopic expression of dominant negative TORTED (Hennig and Neufeld, 2002) resulted in significantly decreased starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies, and these flies did not respond to HFD (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D using genetic manipulation.

claim: Rapamycin feeding suppressed starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
source: Like TORTED expression in AKHR+ neurons, rapamycin feeding suppressed starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 using pharmacological treatment.

claim: Rapamycin feeding enhanced the baseline locomotion of fed flies.
source: Notably, unlike TORTED expression AKHR+ neurons, rapamycin feeding enhanced the baseline locomotion of fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that global suppression of TOR signaling may have a locomotor effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, with inference about the mechanism.

claim: RNAi knock-down of TSC1 in AKHR+ neurons resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
source: Besides, we genetically activated TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of TSC1, a suppressor of TOR signaling (Wullschleger et al., 2006) and by the ectopic expression of a dominant negative form of AMPK (AMPKDN) (Wullschleger et al., 2006). Both manipulations resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claim: Ectopic expression of a dominant negative form of AMPK (AMPKDN) in AKHR+ neurons resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
source: Besides, we genetically activated TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of TSC1, a suppressor of TOR signaling (Wullschleger et al., 2006) and by the ectopic expression of a dominant negative form of AMPK (AMPKDN) (Wullschleger et al., 2006). Both manipulations resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claim: Only one of the three lipoproteins, named Lipid Transfer Particle (LTP), but not the other two [Lipophorin (LPP) and Microsomal Triglyceride Transfer Protein (MTP)], was significantly upregulated in HFD-fed flies vs. ND-fed flies.
source: We performed proteomic analysis of circulating proteins in flies' hemolymph by mass spectrometry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 2) and found that only one of the three lipoproteins, named Lipid Transfer Particle (LTP), but not the other two [Lipophorin (LPP) and Microsomal Triglyceride Transfer Protein (MTP)], was significantly upregulated in HFD-fed flies vs. ND-fed flies (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B using mass spectrometry.

claim: Both triglycerides and cholesterol were enriched in the hemolymph of HFD-fed flies.
source: Meanwhile, both triglycerides and cholesterol were enriched in the hemolymph of HFD-fed flies (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D using biochemical assays.

claim: Among seven identified lipophorin receptors in Drosophila, lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1) was most abundantly expressed in AKHR+ neurons.
source: To this aim, we carried out single cell RNAseq analysis for individual AKHR+ neurons harvested from the fly brains in situ. Among seven identified lipophorin receptors in Drosophila, lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1) was most abundantly expressed in AKHR+ neurons (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E using single-cell RNAseq.

claim: RNAi knock-down of LpR1 in AKHR+ neurons eliminated the effect of HFD on AKHR accumulation.
source: We thus examined the potential role of LpR1 in mediating the effect of HFD feeding on AKHR accumulation and starvation-induced hyperactivity. RNAi knock-down of LpR1 in AKHR+ neurons eliminated the effect of HFD on AKHR accumulation (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-G using genetic manipulation.

claim: Flies with LpR1 knockdown in AKHR+ neurons did not respond to HFD feeding with an enhancement of starvation-induced hyperactivity.
source: Consistently, these flies did not respond to HFD feeding with an enhancement of starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H using behavioral assays.

claim: Knocking down LpR1 in the fat body generated diet-independent hyperlipidemia in ND-fed flies.
source: By knocking down LpR1 in the fat body, the major organ for lipid storage and metabolism (Zheng et al., 2016), we generated diet-independent hyperlipidemia in ND-fed flies (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claim: Compared with the control group, the phosphorylation of p70S6K in the diet-independent hyperlipidemia group was significantly up-regulated.
source: We then asked whether diet-independent hyperlipidemia had similar effects on AKHR accumulation and starvation-induced hyperactivity as HFD feeding. Compared with the control group, the phosphorylation of p70S6K in the diet-independent hyperlipidemia group was significantly up-regulated (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C-D using western blot analysis.

claim: Diet-independent hyperlipidemia led to upregulated AKHR accumulation.
source: In addition, diet-independent hyperlipidemia led to upregulated AKHR accumulation (Figure 8E–F), mimicking the effect of HFD feeding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E-F using western blot analysis.

claim: ND-fed, hyperlipidemic flies showed significantly stronger starvation-induced hyperactivity than the two control groups.
source: Consistent with these results, these ND-fed, hyperlipidemic flies showed significantly stronger starvation-induced hyperactivity than the two control groups (Figure 8G), which was comparable to that of HFD-fed flies (Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8G using behavioral assays.

claim: Starvation-induced hyperactivity in the fruit fly is composed of two behavioral components: increased sensitivity to food cues, and enhanced exploratory locomotion.
source: Conceptually, food-seeking behavior in the fruit fly is composed of two behavioral components, increased sensitivity to food cues, and enhanced exploratory locomotion, which altogether facilitates the localization and acquisition of desirable food sources (Root et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AKH acts as a hunger signal to activate its cognate receptor AKHR expressed in the fat body and subsequently triggers lipid mobilization and energy allocation.
source: As an insect counterpart of mammalian glucagon, AKH acts as a hunger signal to activate its cognate receptor AKHR expressed in the fat body and subsequently triggers lipid mobilization and energy allocation (Bharucha et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: OA+AKHR+ neurons are functionally analogous to mammalian NPY/AgRP neurons in the hypothalamus.
source: In that sense, these OA+AKHR+ neurons are functionally analogous to mammalian NPY/AgRP neurons in the hypothalamus, which also senses organismal metabolic states and regulates specific food intake behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference based on functional similarities between the two neuronal populations.

claim: HFD feeding in mammals increases the excitability of NPY/AgRP neurons, which contributes to the hypersensitivity to starvation and increased food consumption.
source: Notably, HFD feeding in mammals also increases the excitability of NPY/AgRP neurons, which contributes to the hypersensitivity to starvation and increased food consumption (Vernia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fasting induces autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons via fatty acid uptake and promotes AgRP expression, which in turn enhances food intake.
source: For example, fasting induces autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons via fatty acid uptake and promotes AgRP expression, which in turn enhances food intake (Kaushik et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Eliminating autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons reduces food intake and hence body weight and fat deposits.
source: In line with these results, eliminating autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons reduces food intake and hence body weight and fat deposits (Kaushik et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of autophagy in POMC neurons displays increased food intake and adiposity.
source: Conversely, loss of autophagy in POMC neurons displays increased food intake and adiposity (Coupé et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HFD suppresses autophagy in different peripheral tissue types such as liver, skeletal muscle, and the adipose tissue.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that HFD suppresses autophagy in different peripheral tissue types such as liver, skeletal muscle, and the adipose tissue (Feng et al., 2016; He et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HFD suppresses autophagy in the hypothalamus.
source: Similarly, HFD suppresses autophagy in the hypothalamus, whereas blocking hypothalamic autophagy, particularly in POMC neurons, exacerbates HFD induced obesity (Coupé et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Blocking hypothalamic autophagy, particularly in POMC neurons, exacerbates HFD induced obesity.
source: Similarly, HFD suppresses autophagy in the hypothalamus, whereas blocking hypothalamic autophagy, particularly in POMC neurons, exacerbates HFD induced obesity (Coupé et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TOR is a highly conserved serine-threonine kinase that controls numerous anabolic cellular processes.
source: TOR, a highly conserved serine-threonine kinase, controls numerous anabolic cellular processes (Proud, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Manipulating AMPK-TOR signaling results in the dysfunction of NPY/AgRP neurons as well as POMC neurons, which leads to abnormal food consumption and adiposity.
source: Similarly, rodent studies have shown that manipulating AMPK-TOR signaling results in the dysfunction of NPY/AgRP neurons as well as POMC neurons, which leads to abnormal food consumption and adiposity (Kong et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chronic over-nutrition, especially excessive intake of dietary lipids, is one of the leading causes of obesity and obesity-associated metabolic disturbances.
source: Chronic over-nutrition, especially excessive intake of dietary lipids, is one of the leading causes of these metabolic disturbances (Bray and Popkin, 1998; Hill et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HFD imposes adverse effects on the physiology and metabolism of liver, skeletal muscle, the adipose tissue, and the nervous system.
source: Accumulating evidence has shown that HFD imposes adverse effects on the physiology and metabolism of liver, skeletal muscle, the adipose tissue, and the nervous system (Dietrich et al., 2013; Gómez-Pérez et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; Shimobayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, particularly neurons expressing Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and Agouti-Related Neuropeptide (AgRP) or those expressing Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), are important behavioral and metabolic regulators.
source: In rodent models, neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, particularly neurons expressing Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and Agouti-Related Neuropeptide (AgRP) or those expressing Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), are important behavioral and metabolic regulators (Belgardt et al., 2009; Ollmann et al., 1997; Stanley and Leibowitz, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NPY/AgRP neurons detect various neural and hormonal cues such as circulating glucose and fatty acids, leptin, and ghrelin, and modulate energy intake and expenditure accordingly.
source: These neurons detect various neural and hormonal cues such as circulating glucose and fatty acids, leptin, and ghrelin, and modulate energy intake and expenditure accordingly (Belgardt et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Upon the reduction of the internal energy state, NPY/AgRP neurons are activated and exert a robust orexigenic effect.
source: Upon the reduction of the internal energy state, NPY/AgRP neurons are activated and exert a robust orexigenic effect (Belgardt et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Genetic ablation of NPY/AgRP neurons in neonatal mice completely abolishes food consumption.
source: Genetic ablation of NPY/AgRP neurons in neonatal mice completely abolishes food consumption whereas acute activation of these neurons significantly enhances food consumption (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Acute activation of NPY/AgRP neurons significantly enhances food consumption.
source: Genetic ablation of NPY/AgRP neurons in neonatal mice completely abolishes food consumption whereas acute activation of these neurons significantly enhances food consumption (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NPY/AgRP neurons antagonize the function of POMC neurons that plays a suppressive role on food consumption.
source: NPY/AgRP neurons also antagonize the function of POMC neurons that plays a suppressive role on food consumption (Roseberry et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HFD increases the intrinsic excitability of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: For example, HFD increases the intrinsic excitability of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons (Vernia et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HFD induces leptin resistance.
source: induces leptin resistance (Mazor et al., 2018; Olofsson et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HFD enhances inhibitory innervations of NPY/AgRP neurons with anorexigenic POMC neurons.
source: and enhances their inhibitory innervations with anorexigenic POMC neurons (Newton et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Maternal HFD, alcohol consumption, and aging disrupt normal food intake via affecting the excitability and/or innervation of NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Interestingly, besides HFD, other metabolic challenges, including maternal HFD, alcohol consumption, as well as aging, also disrupt normal food intake via affecting the excitability and/or innervation of NPY/AgRP neurons (Cains et al., 2017; Füredi et al., 2018; Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NPY/AgRP neurons play a role in food-seeking behavior.
source: It has been reported that NPY/AgRP neurons also play a role in food-seeking behavior (Aponte et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Food seeking and food consumption are temporally and spatially separated and even reciprocally inhibited.
source: However, to ensure adequate food intake, food seeking and food consumption are temporally and spatially separated and even reciprocally inhibited (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fruit flies Drosophila melanogaster share fundamental analogy to vertebrate counterparts on the regulation of energy homeostasis and organismal metabolism.
source: Fruit flies Drosophila melanogaster share fundamental analogy to vertebrate counterparts on the regulation of energy homeostasis and organismal metabolism despite that they diverged several hundred million years ago (Pandey and Nichols, 2011; Rajan and Perrimon, 2013; Reiter et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fruit flies exhibited robust starvation-induced hyperactivity that was directed towards the localization and acquisition of food sources.
source: Our previous work showed that fruit flies exhibited robust starvation-induced hyperactivity that was directed towards the localization and acquisition of food sources, therefore resembling an important aspect of food-seeking behavior upon starvation (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A small subset of OA neurons in the fly brain specifically regulated starvation-induced hyperactivity.
source: We also identified a small subset of OA neurons in the fly brain that specifically regulated starvation-induced hyperactivity (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Neuropeptide F (NPF), short NPF (sNPF), Leucokinin, and Allatostatin A (AstA) have been shown to regulate food consumption in fruit flies, all of which have known mammalian homologs that regulate food intake.
source: Among them, Neuropeptide F (NPF), short NPF (sNPF), Leucokinin, and Allatostatin A (AstA), have been shown to regulate food consumption, all of which have known mammalian homologs that regulate food intake (Pool and Scott, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Starvation-induced hyperactivity is regulated by two classes of neuroendocrine cells: one functionally analogous to pancreatic α cells that produce AKH upon starvation, and another that produces Drosophila insulin-like peptides (DILPs), resembling the function of pancreatic β cells.
source: In particular, starvation-induced hyperactivity is regulated by two classes of neuroendocrine cells (Yu et al., 2016). One is functionally analogous to pancreatic α cells and produce AKH upon starvation, whereas the other produces Drosophila insulin-like peptides (DILPs), resembling the function of pancreatic β cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: AKH and DILPs exert antagonistic functions on starvation-induced hyperactivity via the same group of OA neurons in the fly brain.
source: These two classes of Drosophila hormones exert antagonistic functions on starvation-induced hyperactivity via the same group of OA neurons in the fly brain (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Excess dietary lipids are transported by a lipoprotein LTP to enter OA+AKHR+ neurons via the cognate receptor LpR1.
source: Upon HFD, excess dietary lipids are transported by a lipoprotein LTP to enter these OA+AKHR+ neurons via the cognate receptor LpR1, which in turn suppresses autophagy-dependent degradation of AKHR.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.
